body_html:
Last week, I sent a trade alert about a new position I added to the portfolio. As promised, here is the full deep dive.

This company does work that most people walk past every day. It builds the stuff that keeps cities moving. The business went through three tough years, then flipped the script this year: back to profit, strong cash generation, and a balance sheet that now leans net-cash.

Why I’m interested, at a glance:

  • Revenue is re-accelerating as multi-year projects ramp.

  • Margins are expanding as newer contracts with better terms take over.

  • Cash flow is strong, even after normal capex.

  • Debt risk is down. Liquidity is up.

  • The stock still trades at a discount to peers on several common metrics.

  • I see a clear path for earnings to be higher again next year if execution holds.

  • My fair-value work points to a +50% upside from here.

I’ll walk you through the story, the numbers, the risks, and the catalysts… and I’ll show how ROIC ties the operating improvements to valuation so you can see exactly why I bought.

Do you want to know?

I still remember my first trip to Manhattan in 2006 with a friend. The city swallowed the week. We ran out of time before we ran out of things to see. In 2013, I went back to work for six months. I finally had time to walk the grid, block by block. Since then, I have flown in a couple of times a year to visit my brother. One thing has been constant.

Manhattan is always under construction.

It is so big and so old that there is always a street torn up or a scaffold going up. After a while, I started noticing the Tutor Perini logo on hard hats and vests.

I was on a midtown sidewalk again, watching commuters stream past a site for the Midtown Bus Terminal Redevelopment. The sign read “Tutor Perini.” Few people know this 130-year-old builder behind some of America’s biggest projects. Fewer still noticed when the stock slumped after years of losses.

That picture is changing.

Tutor Perini has doubled its backlog to a record $21.1 billion and is back to making money. The share price has already jumped this year, and I still see room to run.

How did this underdog turn into a real contender for a top stock pick?

Here is the story.

TLDR

Tutor Perini (TPC) is a heavy construction contractor that’s staging a comeback. After three years of big losses (over $160 million lost in 2024 ) and a beaten-down stock, Tutor Perini’s fundamentals have dramatically improved in 2025. The company’s backlog of projects (mostly public infrastructure) hit a record $21.1 billion in Q2 2025 (double last year’s), and these new contracts carry higher profit margins. Revenue is growing double-digits, and margins are expanding.

In the latest quarter, TPC generated its second best cash flow ever ($262 million in Q2) and now has more cash than debt on its balance sheet for the first time since 2010. Management raised earnings guidance and expects 2026–2027 earnings to exceed 2025’s.

Yet the stock, around $60 today, still trades at less than 6x FCF, a discount to peers. My DCF model gives a ~$92 fair value per share, suggesting significant upside.

Keep reading if you want the full story…

Table of Contents:

  • Company History & Evolution

  • How Tutor Perini Makes Money (Unit Economics & Drivers)

  • Industry Landscape, Growth Levers & Outlook

  • Competitors and Tutor Perini’s Edge

  • Management Quality & Capital Allocation

  • Financials

  • Valuation & ROIC

  • Key Risks, Bear Case & Variant View

  • Catalysts

  • Verdict: From Underdog to Top Pick

Company History & Evolution

Tutor Perini’s roots date back to the 19th century. The “Perini” side was founded in 1894 by Bonfiglio Perini, an Italian stonemason who built a New England construction business. Over the decades, Perini Corporation became known for large civil works like roads and tunnels.

Meanwhile, in 1949, Albert Tutor started a family construction firm in California. His son, Ronald Tutor, joined in 1963 and later partnered with N.M. Saliba to form Tutor-Saliba, which focused on big, complex projects.

By the late 20th century, Ron Tutor saw an opportunity to combine forces with Perini. He led a recapitalization of Perini in 1997 and eventually merged Tutor-Saliba and Perini in 2008, creating Tutor Perini Corporation.

Today, Tutor Perini is a diversified construction contractor with more than 20 subsidiaries across the U.S. and abroad.

It operates through three main segments.

  • Civil: Large public infrastructure projects (bridges, highways, transit systems, waterworks, etc.). The Civil segment generated ~49% of revenue in 2024 and has historically been the profit engine. Tutor Perini often bids as a prime contractor or joint venture on massive civil jobs. Examples include the California high-speed rail project and Los Angeles subway extensions, each worth billions.

  • Building: Construction of commercial buildings, specialty public facilities, and private developments (airports, casinos, hospitals, schools, etc.). This segment was ~37% of 2024 revenue. Notable projects include skyscrapers, hotels (Tutor Perini built the Cosmopolitan Resort in Las Vegas), courthouses, and tech campuses. Building projects tend to be lower-margin but important for diversifying revenue.

  • Specialty Contractors: Installation of electrical, mechanical, plumbing, and fire protection systems, as well as concrete and steel work, often on Tutor Perini’s own jobs. This segment was ~14% of 2024 revenue . It includes subsidiaries like Fisk Electric and Five Star Electric (electrical contracting) and Lunda Construction (specialty civil work like bridges). Having in-house specialty trade capability lets Tutor Perini self-perform critical work, which can improve control and, ideally, profitability.

Over its evolution, Tutor Perini grew by acquiring regional contractors to bolster these segments. For example, it bought GreenStar (mechanical), Fisk Electric, Lunda, and others in the 2000s and 2010s, broadening its geographic reach and expertise.

Tutor Perini has a broad national presence, with active operations in key regions like California, Nevada and New York, plus international work in places such as Canada and the Middle East. This footprint allows the company to pursue large projects in multiple geographies where infrastructure demand is strongest.

However, growing into a $5 billion-plus revenue company wasn’t without growing pains. TPC became known for taking on very large, complex projects, the kind that often come with disputes and cost overruns in construction. By the late 2010s, the company had several legacy projects that turned unprofitable.

Management (led by Ron Tutor as CEO at the time) was aggressive in pursuing claims for additional compensation on troubled jobs, leading to long legal battles with project owners. This strategy sometimes backfired when arbitrators or courts ruled against TPC, forcing the company to write off revenues it had booked but not yet collected. These write-downs contributed to steep losses.

The stock got hammered, hitting a low of around $5 in late 2022.

It all culminated in three consecutive annual net losses: –$210 million in 2022, –$171 million in 2023, and –$164 million in 2024.

TPC’s reputation in the market was that of a contractor that won big jobs but often struggled to get paid what it expected, leading to volatile earnings.

Amid this turmoil, a leadership transition quietly took place. Longtime CEO Ronald Tutor (now in his 80s) handed day-to-day control to Gary Smalley, a veteran CFO who became President in 2023 and CEO on January 1, 2025. Ron Tutor remains Executive Chairman (through 2026) and still owns a significant stake, but the new CEO’s mandate is to improve execution and financial performance. Smalley’s style comes across as more measured and focused on cash flow and risk management (as we’ll see in the latest results).

This leadership change set the stage for Tutor Perini’s current revival.

How Tutor Perini Makes Money (Unit Economics & Drivers)

TPC’s revenue comes from construction contracts, primarily fixed-price or guaranteed maximum price contracts for government agencies and private owners. The company bids on a project with an estimated cost; if they win, they get paid that amount (with some adjustments for change orders), and their profit is whatever is left after actual costs.

This model puts the onus on TPC to execute efficiently and manage risks like material cost inflation or site delays. If actual costs exceed the bid, TPC can lose money unless they successfully negotiate change orders or claims for additional funds.

About 72% of Tutor Perini’s revenue in 2024 came from public sector clients (state, local, or federal government). Governments often select contractors via competitive bidding, where the lowest responsible bid wins. This fosters a razor-thin margin environment. Tutor Perini’s unit economics historically were challenging: gross margins in low-to-mid single digits on many projects. One large mistake can wipe out profits. This was evident in the Specialty segment, which had a –10% operating margin in Q2 2025 due to legacy losses.

However, there are a few key drivers that allow TPC to make money:

  • Scale & Self-Performance: Because TPC is a top-tier builder with its own specialty trades, it can handle mega-projects that smaller contractors cannot. Its Civil segment thrives on scale. A $1 billion subway extension involves complex tunnelling, concrete, and systems integration, which TPC can perform or oversee directly. These big jobs carry higher potential margins (10–15%+ at the project level) to compensate for their complexity. When executed well, they generate outsized profits. The company’s strategy is to leverage this scale advantage to win marquee projects with fewer competitors (or sometimes none, as I’ll discuss) and price in a healthy margin.

  • Contract Mix & Risk Management: TPC has been more selective about contract terms after learning from past missteps. Management now emphasizes pursuing work with “improved terms”. For instance, contracts that include escalation clauses for materials or more owner contingency for surprises. They also balance some fixed-price work with cost-plus contracts (where the client reimburses costs plus a fee). In 2024, a meaningful chunk of revenue came from cost-plus jobs, which carry lower risk (though also lower margins). This mix helps stabilize earnings.

  • Backlog Quality: Not all revenue dollars are equal. TPC’s recent backlog additions are said to be higher-margin projects with better economics than the legacy work-off. As the CEO puts it, “Our backlog has continued to grow and includes various larger, long-duration and higher-margin projects, most of which are in the early stages”. Essentially, new projects starting now were bid under more favourable conditions (post-COVID pricing, funding from new infrastructure programs, and less competition). This bodes well for unit economics going forward, as these projects should contribute fatter margins in the coming years.

  • Project Execution & Contingency: Construction margin is a function of controlling costs. TPC appears to be executing better lately. For example, in Q2 2025, the Civil segment had favourable cost adjustments of $28 million from change orders and improved performance. Management also builds contingencies into bids and the company’s guidance. For 2025, they noted the earnings outlook still carries a “significant amount of contingency for unknown or unanticipated developments”. This means if things go smoothly, actual results could exceed forecasts. It’s a conservative approach to protect profitability.

Let’s talk numbers on unit economics: In 2024, Tutor Perini had $4.3 billion in revenue and gross profit of about $130 million (roughly 3% gross margin). Operating margin was even worse due to high SG&A and those big write-offs from disputes, resulting in net losses.

But fast forward to 2025: the Civil segment’s operating margin is now ~15% (up from ~8–10% a few years ago). This is a huge improvement, reflecting that new civil jobs are being bid with higher expected profit. Even the Building segment, historically sub-5% margin, delivered 4.8% operating margin in Q2 2025 (income of $22m on $462m revenue), its best since 2011. Specialty contracting is still catching up (it had an $18m loss in Q2 due to remaining legacy claims ), but management expects Specialty to break even by year-end and eventually reach 5–8% margins once old disputes are resolved.

Industry Landscape, Growth Levers & Outlook

Tutor Perini sits within the construction & engineering industry, specifically focusing on large-scale projects. 2025 has been a boon for this industry in the U.S. after years of underinvestment. A few macro tailwinds and industry dynamics are crucial:

Infrastructure Spending Boom

The U.S. Bipartisan Infrastructure Law (enacted late 2021) is pumping $1.2 trillion into infrastructure over 5 years. Funds are flowing into transit systems, bridges, highways, and water projects, exactly Tutor Perini’s wheelhouse. We’re seeing this translate into project awards in 2023–2025.

For instance, TPC’s record backlog includes projects like a new $3.9 billion California high-speed rail segment and a $3.7 billion Los Angeles subway extension. These government-funded projects will keep many civil contractors busy for the next decade. Tutor Perini is already benefitting: its Q2 2025 civil revenue was record-high and up 34% y/y.

Limited Competition for Mega-Projects

The heavy construction market has high barriers to entry. You need bonding capacity, specialized expertise, and a track record to even bid on multi-billion-dollar jobs. Many public companies in engineering (e.g. AECOM, Jacobs) have actually exited fixed-price construction in recent years to focus on design and consulting, due to the risks.

Others, like Fluor and Granite, have been more selective or focused on different niches (energy for Fluor, smaller scale for Granite). This has left a narrow field of competitors for the largest projects.

According to Tutor’s management during the Q2 2026 earnings call,

We have never seen more than 1 other bidder in the last 2 years. And on 1 occasion, 2 occasions, we were the only bidder. So yes, nothing's changed. The competition is minimal.

That’s a striking insight: TPC often faces just one competitor (or none) on billion-dollar bids. Less competition means they can command better pricing and terms. Indeed, Ron Tutor noted nothing has changed about this dynamic, it remains a seller’s market for big civil contractors. This industry shift is a huge growth lever for TPC’s margins and win rate.

Steady Flow of New Contracts

The project pipeline is robust. TPC’s management says they have a “full pipeline of opportunities” and can afford to be selective on new work. Even after doubling the backlog, they continue to win jobs. A few examples from just the past summer: a $1.87 billion contract for a new bus storage facility in New York City (part of the Midtown Bus Terminal redevelopment), a $220 million casino expansion contract in California, and multiple highway and bridge projects in Minnesota totalling ~$100 million.

This steady drumbeat of awards shows that demand is not the constraint. TPC is capturing projects across the country, from transit hubs in NYC to casinos and hospitals. The company expects backlog to remain strong through 2025, aided by Building segment projects currently in pre-construction that will convert to signed contracts later in the year. More backlog means more fuel for future revenue growth.

Secular Trends & Federal Support

The push to modernize infrastructure (transit, rail, airports), build resiliency (water, power systems), and even trends like clean energy and semiconductor fabs all generate construction projects.

TPC is mainly civil-focused, but it can benefit indirectly if, say, new chip plants require surrounding infrastructure or new federal facilities are built. Notably, federal spending on transit and transportation is rising, and TPC’s projects often receive Federal Transit Administration (FTA) funds.

Ron Tutor highlighted that “there’s more and more money going into transit, which is our biggest strength… we’re the beneficiary of that.” This outlook suggests a multi-year growth runway. In fact, management stated they expect double-digit revenue growth for multiple years due to the record backlog, and they foresee 2026 and 2027 EPS exceeding 2025’s increased guidance.

The company said approximately $4.5 billion of its backlog at the end of 2024 is expected to turn into 2025 revenue, and with more awards since, 2025 could even top that. Beyond 2025, if even half of the $21 billion backlog converts over, say, 3 years, that’s ~$7 billion per year of potential revenue, a huge step up. Practically, revenue will ramp as mega-projects hit peak construction (often 2–3 years after award). Many of TPC’s big new projects are in early phases (design, mobilization) and will ramp in 2025–2027, fueling growth.

The industry also faces constraints like labour availability and the supply chain. Paradoxically, those can help incumbents because owners prefer experienced contractors who can navigate shortages. TPC has 7,500 employees and relationships with specialty subcontractors, which should help in a tight labour market. They also pre-purchase materials to lock in costs.

For example, management noted they’ve “done a very good job buying out materials and subs” on projects to mitigate inflation and tariffs, passing the risk onto vendors by locking prices. This proactive approach means potential material cost spikes (e.g. new import tariffs) shouldn’t derail their project economics. This is an important consideration in the current inflationary environment.

Competitors and Tutor Perini’s Edge

TPC’s competitors vary by segment:

  • In Civil (infrastructure), main peers include Kiewit, Bechtel, Skanska, Dragados, Fluor, Granite Construction (GVA), and some regional firms. Notably, Kiewit and Bechtel are private giants often bidding on similar mega-projects. Skanska (a Swedish firm) and Dragados (Spanish) also pursue big U.S. projects, especially in transit and rail. Granite is a public company, but focuses more on highways and mid-sized jobs. Fluor (FLR) is public and huge, but much of its business is energy/industrial; still, Fluor sometimes bids on infrastructure consortia.

  • In Building (vertical construction), competitors include large general contractors like AECOM’s former construction arm, Turner Construction (private), Clark Construction (private), Gilbane, DPR, and various regional builders. However, Tutor Perini often targets specialized buildings (e.g. casinos, courthouses, hospitals) where clients may choose based on specific expertise and past relationships. For instance, in hospitality construction, peers might be AECOM Hunt or PCL Construction.

  • In Specialty contracting, competition is with local contractors in the electrical, mechanical trades. TPC’s subsidiaries, like Fisk Electric, compete with other specialty firms for subcontracting jobs. But since much of their work is internal (on Tutor’s own projects), the competitive dynamic is a bit different – more about efficiency than winning third-party work.

Given this landscape, what is TPC’s edge? I see a few differentiators:

Edge #1. Ability to Build Anything (Scale & Technical Know-How)

TPC is one of the few U.S. contractors that can build both a skyscraper and a subway tunnel. Its portfolio ranges from the Hudson Yards development in NYC to the Purple Line subway in LA to military bases and airports. This breadth and scale give it a seat at the table for mega-projects that smaller firms literally couldn’t handle.

In practical terms, this means when a city is approving a multi-billion-dollar project, Tutor Perini is likely on the short list. This edge has been reinforced by the exit of some public competitors from fixed-price contracting. The company is now one of the last men standing for giant civil jobs.

As I highlighted earlier, they’ve often been the sole bidder on recent large tenders. That’s a major competitive advantage: if owners have no alternative (or only one alternative) for a project, TPC can negotiate better pricing and contract terms.

Edge #2. Integrated Capabilities (Self-Performing Trades)

Tutor Perini’s ownership of specialty contractors means it can self-perform key portions of work instead of subcontracting everything out. For example, on a rail project, its Lunda Construction unit might do the concrete and bridges, while Fisk Electric installs the power systems.

This integration can improve coordination and margins. The profit that would normally go to an outside subcontractor can be kept in-house. It also provides more control over scheduling and quality, which is vital on complex jobs. Few competitors have this breadth under one roof. Many big contractors rely entirely on subs, which can introduce execution risk.

TPC’s model, if managed well, is an edge in delivering complicated projects on time. (To be fair, it also means they bear more direct cost risk, but the recent strategy of locking in material prices and careful bidding mitigates that.)

Edge #3. Niche Strengths and Track Record

In certain niches, TPC is the go-to contractor. For example, in building gaming and hospitality projects (casinos, resorts), TPC has decades of experience as it has built notable Las Vegas landmarks.

In mass transit and underground construction, few U.S. firms have done as many large tunnelling jobs (Tutor-Saliba’s legacy and current JV on NYC’s East Side Access tunnel show that expertise). This track record gives confidence to project owners. When California needed teams for high-speed rail segments, Tutor Perini was on winning teams largely because of its resume in complex civil works.

Competitors might excel in one category but not cover all; TPC’s broad resume is an edge when projects span multiple types (e.g. a design-build of an airport terminal with civil and building elements).

Edge #4. Strong Relationships & Subsidiary Network

With +20 subsidiaries nationwide, TPC maintains local presence and relationships. For instance, in California, Tutor Perini’s building subsidiary Rudolph and Sletten takes on many of the tricky general‐contracting projects. And in New York City, its specialty firm Five Star Electric dominates big electrical jobs.

These subsidiaries carry their own brand reputation but benefit from the parent’s financial backing. This network can outflank competitors by offering a “one-stop shop” or a joint bid where multiple Tutor Perini units collaborate.

Also, longstanding client relationships (like with the U.S. military or certain state DOTs) mean repeat business. Smaller competitors might not have the financial capacity or bonding to handle repeat giant projects.

In summary, TPC’s edge is being the “last big generalist contractor” in an industry that has seen specialization and retrenchment. One can think of Tutor Perini as having a quasi-oligopoly position in segments like large transit infrastructure. Not a monopoly, but perhaps one of maybe 3 serious bidders in the U.S. for a multi-billion transit hub.

That’s powerful in a high-demand market.

Management Quality & Capital Allocation

Tutor Perini’s management has a mixed history, but recent changes are encouraging. Ronald Tutor, the long-time CEO and current Executive Chairman, is an industry legend known for his bold deal-making and tenacity in dispute battles.

However, his aggressive style arguably contributed to the company’s woes (taking on too much risk, booking revenue before resolution of claims, etc.). The new CEO, Gary Smalley, comes from a finance background (CFO since 2015) and appears focused on operational discipline and transparency.

For example, one of his first moves was to begin reporting adjusted earnings excluding volatile share-based compensation expense, to give a clearer picture of underlying performance. This suggests a shareholder-friendly approach to communication.

On the latest earnings call, management’s tone was confident but measured. Smalley repeatedly emphasized contingencies and not getting ahead of themselves, even as results excelled (“so far, so excellent,” he said).

They raised guidance for 2025, but noted it still includes a cushion for unknowns. This conservatism marks a shift from the past, where guidance often proved too optimistic. It reflects better risk management, acknowledging the uncertainties in construction.

Capital allocation under this management is primarily about strengthening the balance sheet and investing in projects, rather than dividends or buybacks. TPC pays no dividend (and hasn’t historically). Given the big losses and debt load of prior years, it was prudent not to return cash to shareholders. Instead, the focus was on reducing debt.

And here management has delivered: through Q2 2025, they turned net debt into net cash. Specifically, total debt stands at $419 million while cash is $526 million, meaning a $107 million net cash position.

This is a remarkable turnaround from a year ago, when net debt was hundreds of millions. They achieved it by using windfall cash from operations to pay down a Term Loan and other borrowings.

In early 2024, they even refinanced their senior notes (issuing a new $400 million bond due 2029) to remove near-term maturity risk. The new bonds carry a high interest rate (~11.875%), but management subsequently paid off other higher-cost debt, like a Term Loan B, to lighten interest expense.

As a result, interest expense should drop to ~$55 million in 2025 from $89 million in 2024, saving over $30 million annually.

With net cash now, what will management do?

Likely, they will still maintain a strong liquidity buffer because the construction business can have wild swings in working capital (funding projects, etc.). I expect no dividend until earnings become steady over a few years. Buybacks are possible if the stock stays low, but again, given growth opportunities, I suspect cash will be conserved for bonding capacity and project investments (e.g. equipment, tech) or perhaps strategic acquisitions.

Tutor Perini hasn’t made big acquisitions in recent years, but if a niche player would bolster a growth area (like a specialty contractor in a region where they see lots of work), they might consider it. However, with such a full plate of projects, internal execution is priority #1.

The management quality can also be judged by how they navigated the tough period and the changes implemented:

  • They resolved or settled several dispute cases (some at a loss, but at least putting them behind). In Q2 2025, they noted progress on settlements without major hits to earnings, implying smarter handling of claims.

  • They decided to eat a higher share-based compensation cost in Q2 (which hurt GAAP profit by $38 million ) because the stock price doubled, but then introduced adjusted EPS to clarify that anomaly. This honesty in financial reporting (instead of trying to ignore the cost entirely) is a positive.

  • They improved working capital dramatically: costs in excess of billings (work done not yet billed) fell from $943 million to $856 million in the first half of 2025, while billings in excess (advance payments from clients) rose from $1.22 billion to $1.68 billion. This indicates management is collecting cash faster and not letting unbilled costs balloon. It’s a sign of negotiating better payment terms and focusing on cash generation. Indeed, operating cash flow hit record highs as a result.

Ron Tutor’s continued presence is a wildcard. He owns 13.2% of shares, and as Executive Chairman, he still influences strategy.

There’s a risk of him pushing for aggressive growth or specific deals. However, the fact that he agreed to transition CEO duties and that guidance is now being raised cautiously suggests he’s on board with the new approach.

Also, Ron Tutor is in his late 70s/early 80s; a long-term investor might consider succession. The plan is that he stays Chair through 2026, after which he may step back entirely. Gary Smalley and CFO Ryan Soroka (who took over as CFO when Smalley became CEO) seem competent and aligned with shareholder interests (improving profitability, transparency, etc.).

Overall, I’d rate management quality as improving. They’ve executed a turnaround so far in 2025, which gives credibility. The test will be sustaining it: delivering projects on budget and on time, and hitting the guidance they’ve put out (which they even increased twice this year, a rarity that signals confidence ).

If they do, it will mark a new chapter where Tutor Perini is seen as a reliable compounder rather than a boom-bust contractor. Importantly, management said they have no need to bid low on projects now, given their backlog cushion. This discipline bodes well for capital allocation in a broader sense (not chasing unprofitable revenue).

Financials

Let’s dig into the numbers. The financial turnaround from 2024 to 2025 is striking:

Revenue Growth

2024 revenue was $4.33 billion, up 12% from 2023 as new work started kicking in.

For 2025, I estimate revenue to be ~$5.3 billion (which would be ~22% growth).

I don’t think my projection is too aggressive. In the first half of 2025, revenue was $2.62 billion vs $2.18 billion in H1 2024 (a 20% increase). Q2 2025 alone was up 22% y/y, the highest quarterly revenue since 2009. It’s clear Tutor Perini is emerging from a slow period and entering a high-growth phase as backlog projects ramp up.

Margins & Profitability

2024 was a net loss, largely due to charge-offs and poor margins on old jobs. But by Q2 2025, profitability returned. Q2 2025 income from construction operations was $76.4 million (5.6% operating margin), up 89% from $40.5 million (3.6% margin) in Q2 2024.

After the heavy share-comp expense and interest/taxes, Q2 GAAP net income was $20.0m (EPS $0.38). That may seem small, but note it includes a $38.5m one-time comp charge. On an adjusted basis (excluding that), Q2 net was $75m (EPS $1.41).

Management’s 2025 EPS guidance is $1.70–$2.00 GAAP, which at ~52.7 million shares outstanding equates to ~$90–$105 million net income. They also gave Adjusted EPS guidance of $3.65–$3.95, which strips out that stock-based comp volatility: showing the underlying earning power is closer to $190–$200m after tax.

I expect margins to keep improving. Civil segment profit is ramping (15% margins now), Building segment is recovering (profitable again), and Specialty is set to break even, then go to mid-single-digit margins by next year.

G&A expense will be a bit higher in 2025 (~$370m) due to stock comp, but aside from that, operating leverage should be significant as revenue grows.

Importantly, interest expense is dropping with debt reduction, and the company has tax loss carryforwards from past losses.

Balance Sheet

At June 30, 2025: Cash $526m, Debt $419m, so net cash ~$107m. A year prior, debt was higher; they refinanced $400m of notes at 11.875% and paid off a $122m term loan.

The current debt mainly consists of $400m bond (due 2029) and some equipment loans. The bond has a high coupon, but with cash on hand, they could consider partial early redemption (though there’s likely a make-whole until 2026).

The balance sheet is solid now. At the end of Q2 2025, Tutor Perini had $3.9 billion in current assets against $3.0 billion in current liabilities, leaving roughly $943 million in net current assets. Cash stood at $526 million, more than covering the $419 million of total debt. Receivables and unbilled costs remain large at over $2.1 billion, but they are roughly balanced by accounts payable and advance billings from clients. The key point is that liquidity is strong and the company is in a net cash position for the first time in over a decade.

There are big “contract assets” and “liabilities” (unbilled vs advance billings), but net working capital is positive.

One red flag to watch: the $856m in costs in excess of billings. This is essentially revenue recognized, but cash not yet collected (often due to disputes). This came down from $942m at 2024’s end, as noted, but is still significant. Management’s confidence and cash flow results suggest a lot of that will eventually be collected or resolved favourably, but it’s an area to keep an eye on.

Cash Flow

This might be the brightest spot. In Q2 2025, Tutor Perini generated $262m operating cash flow, the 2nd best quarter in TPC’s history.

They achieved this through excellent working capital management. Notably, collecting on new projects and some dispute resolutions. The press release said only a “much lesser extent” of the cash came from dispute settlements, and largely from new project collections.

This implies the core business is now throwing off cash, not just one-time catch-ups. The company expects continued strong cash flow in H2 2025, which could mean full-year operating cash well above net income (since some cash is from working capital unwind).

Free cash flow will be a bit lower due to capex. Capex was $57m in H1 2025, likely ~$120–$130 m for full year as guided during the earnings call. This has been higher than historical levels as they’ve been investing in equipment, etc.

Even so, free cash might be $200 million in 2025, which could be used to further pay down debt or just accumulate for future needs. Given the cyclical nature, having a cash cushion is wise.

Valuation & ROIC

Relative Valuation

Looking across the construction peer set, TPC still looks discounted even after its big run. On a forward basis, TPC trades at 18.5x FY1 non-GAAP P/E, falling to 10.3x by FY3 as backlog-driven earnings ramp. That’s a clear discount to peers such as Argan (26.1x FY1, 20.5x FY3), MYR Group (25.4x, 18.5x), and Centuri (35.0x, 19.2x). Even Granite (19.4x, 15.0x) and AECOM (24.1x, 20.1x) fetch higher multiples.

On EV/EBITDA, TPC sits at 10.1x forward, well below Argan (15.9x), MYRG (12.6×), and ACM (15.3x), and roughly in line with Granite (9.4x). Fluor screens at 12.8x but its business mix is skewed toward energy.

EV/Sales tells the same story. TPC trades at just 0.69x trailing, while Argan (2.4x) and MYR (0.81x) command richer valuations. Granite (1.1x) and Centuri (1.1x) are closer but still higher. Historically, TPC’s thin margins have held its multiple down. But with civil margins now running mid-teens, a rerating closer to 1x sales looks realistic. On $5–6 billion in revenue, that would imply a $5–6 billion market cap, well above today’s ~$3.1 billion.

Even on Price to Free Cash Flow, TPC stands out. It trades at just 5.6x, while peers command much richer multiples: Argan at 21.0x, MYR Group at 25.8x, Granite at 17.4x, Centuri at 14.2x, Fluor at 28.5x, and AECOM at 20.3x. That gap highlights just how deeply discounted TPC remains relative to its cash-generating power.

The peer comparison reinforces the thesis: Tutor Perini has lagged in valuation because of legacy losses, but as profitability normalizes, it has significant room to close the gap with rivals.

Multiples show TPC is still discounted. To test if that discount makes sense, I look at returns on invested capital.

ROIC

As I mentioned in the latest Weekly, I will start discussing ROIC in my deep dives rather than keeping it behind the scenes. My goal is to show how ROIC links the fundamentals of the company and industry to the valuation.

I like to break ROIC into two parts: NOPAT margin and sales to invested capital. Refer to my ROIC Explained for details.

Sustainable NOPAT margin.

The backlog is richer and carries better terms. Civil is running near mid-teens operating margin, and Building has turned the corner. Management is buying out materials early and locking prices with subs. Specialty is moving toward breakeven.

A 12.5% gross margin assumption is not out of line with industry benchmarks. Construction Financial Management Association (CFMA) data shows that general contractors typically operate in the 12–16% gross margin range, depending on mix and contract type. That means TPC, with a healthier backlog, tighter bidding competition, and more self-perform capability, is simply converging toward what is normal for well-run peers rather than reaching for an unrealistic stretch.

Peers reinforce the case. Granite (GVA) and MYR Group (MYRG) have consistently posted gross margins in the low-teens, showing that large contractors with clean execution and disciplined bidding can sustain profitability at those levels. If TPC executes on its record backlog under improved terms, a sustainable 12.5% gross margin looks well within reach.

SG&A currently runs ~6% of revenue for TPC, which is in line with peers like Granite (6.2%) and MYR Group (5.4%). Centuri operates lower at ~2.9%, while AECOM and Fluor sit under 1% because they allocate overhead differently.

Industry benchmarks show that best-in-class EPCs can operate with sub-5% SG&A, and larger contractors often achieve 3–4% through scale and shared services. As TPC grows into its record $21B backlog, the company should gain operating leverage, pushing SG&A closer to 4% of revenue over time.

Taken together, a 12.5% gross margin and 4% SG&A leave an EBIT margin of 8.5%. Using the 5-year average tax rate of 23% gives a NOPAT margin of 6.5%.

Sales to invested capital.

Tutor Perini has historically run sales-to-invested-capital at about 2.0x on average, a reflection of weak working capital discipline and legacy problem jobs.

That is now changing. Costs in excess of billings are falling, billings in excess are rising, and cash conversion just hit records. Capex remains light at ~1–2% of sales, and the mix is shifting toward long-duration civil jobs where TPC can self-perform more work and keep tighter control of schedules. Those factors support structurally higher asset turns going forward.

The graph above tracks asset utilization (sales/assets), which isn’t identical to sales-to-capital but serves as a useful proxy. You can see how TPC has consistently run at the low end of the peer group (just over 1.0x) versus Granite (~1.3x), Fluor (~1.9x), and MYR (~2.2x). That underperformance fits with TPC’s history of under-managed working capital. With a new management team emphasizing contract discipline and execution, I believe 2.5x sales-to-capital is reasonable on a steady-state basis, marking a clear improvement from the past.

Supporting this view, McKinsey’s benchmarking on engineering and construction firms shows that best-in-class EPCs can run materially higher asset utilization by tightening receivables, controlling unbilled costs, and shifting to self-perform models.

Multiply the 6.5% NOPAT margin times the 2.5x capital turns, and you arrive at a ROIC near 16.4%.

What does the target price imply?

At a $92 share price, the implied EV/IC is about 2.2x. Using a 9.3% WACC, that EV/IC and a 16.4% ROIC back into a long-term growth rate of ~3% by the standard EVA bridge.

Given the industry backdrop, the record backlog, and a healthier bid pipeline, a 3% terminal growth rate looks reasonable.

DCF Model

To get a more concrete handle, I built a DCF model based on the backlog and assumed growth and margins. Here are the key assumptions and results:

Revenue growth

22% in 2025 (to $5.28B), then 13% in 2026 ($5.97B), 11% in 2027 ($6.65B), gradually tapering to ~5% by 2030 and ~2.5% by 2035.

This reflects strong backlog-fueled growth for a few years, then industry growth normalizing to low single digits long-term.

By the 2030s, annual revenue in the model is around $10 billion, which presumes Tutor Perini continues to win its share of projects beyond the current backlog. This is a reasonable scenario if infrastructure spending remains robust.

Margins

I assumed gross margin rises to mid-12% in 2025–2028 (consistent with management aiming for low-double-digit project margins), then slightly tapers to ~10.8% by the terminal period (to be conservative).

SG&A is about 7% of sales. Then I normalized the high comp base, and I gradually tapered it to 4%, assuming no major inefficiencies creep in. That yields an EBITDA margin around 6–8%.

WACC (Discount Rate)

I used a WACC of 9.3%, reflecting a somewhat elevated cost of equity for a small-cap cyclical firm, plus its debt cost. If anything, as the company de-risks, one could argue for a lower WACC, but 9.3% is fine for now.

Other assumptions

The model assumes a 25% effective tax rate in 2025. After that, the rate steps down to the 5-average of 23%. On working capital, I assume Days Receivables of about 190-195, reflecting that the company will continue collecting on older project overages and not let receivables balloon. Days Payables stay stable around 60, which is consistent with past practice. Taken together, these assumptions imply management won’t allow “costs in excess of billings” (unbilled revenue) to swell again as they did in prior years.

Capex 2.3% of revenue in 2025 and gradually converging to 1.3%, which is consistent with historical needs (heavy civil requires equipment, but they also lease a lot). No dividends (retained earnings invested), which matches the company's stance.

Thus, $92 in my view bakes in the current known growth and some continued execution, but not perfection. It corresponds to roughly 0.9x EV/Sales in 2025 and 0.8x in 2027 sales, which is still below general market levels for an established contractor with strong cash flows.

One cannot value Tutor Perini without considering the risk adjustments (which leads to the next section), but purely on a fundamental cash flow basis, the stock looks undervalued. The recent rally (it’s up ~157% YTD) has removed the ultra-deep-value status it had at $15, but it still seems priced for a lot of skepticism.

The variant view (bull case) is that this is now a growth story with improving quality, deserving a higher valuation.

Key Risks, Bear Case & Variant View

Every investment has risks, and TPC is no exception. In fact, a construction contractor has plenty of them.

Risk #1. Project Execution & Fixed-Price Risk

The biggest risk is that Tutor Perini hits trouble on its major projects, such as delays, cost overruns, etc. With so many large jobs in the backlog, statistically, some will encounter issues.

If costs blow out beyond what’s covered in the contract, the company faces losses or protracted claims. This has happened before: e.g., Tutor Perini’s past losses were driven by problem projects where they didn’t get paid for all their work.

A bear would say, “Sure, they have a $21B backlog, but will it be a profitable backlog? Or will history repeat with write-downs?” Even management admits that not all backlog revenue may be realized as profit if the scope is cut or disputes arise.

A related risk: some backlog could be cancelled or delayed (though cancellation is rare in public infrastructure, delays do happen). If a few of the largest projects (those $2–3B ones) go south, it could wipe out the anticipated earnings gains. The bear case argues that construction is an inherently low-margin, unpredictable business. TPC might plan for 5% margins but end up with 0% on some big jobs if things go awry.

Risk #2. Legal and Claims Risks

Tutor Perini is involved in numerous legal proceedings as a normal course of business. It’s almost a running joke that TPC ends up in court with project owners. If they lose a major case or arbitration, it can mean a sudden hit to earnings (non-cash, but still a hit to equity).

For example, in October 2024, an adverse arbitration on a legacy dispute forced a write-down (the 10-K references an unexpected loss on a claim).

If bears are right that a chunk of those uncollected claims are never going to be collected, TPC could still face write-offs that reduce GAAP earnings or even cash if they had to pay damages. Basically, legacy baggage risk remains until those old claims (many in the Specialty segment) are fully resolved.

Management’s counter is that these are normal disputes, and if they lose, it’s a non-cash accounting adjustment since the work was done long ago. But it still affects reported profits and could hurt stock sentiment.

Risk #3. Macroeconomic and Funding Risk

Construction is cyclical. A recession or government budget crisis could slow down project awards or even pause ongoing work. Roughly 77% of TPC’s backlog is with state and local agencies. If state budgets get strained (perhaps due to lower tax revenues in a recession), new projects might be postponed.

Federal funding is somewhat insulated (the infrastructure bill is already allocated), but a future administration could redirect priorities, or if inflation drives project costs up, some projects might scale back scope. The bear case might say: “We’re one election away from a freeze on transit funding” or “States might cancel fancy projects if the economy tanks.”

There’s also interest rate risk. Higher rates could discourage private investment in big developments (though private is only ~15% of backlog now). Additionally, inflation in construction materials or labour, if not hedged, can squeeze margins. Tutor Perini appears to be handling this (locking in prices, etc. ), but unexpected cost inflation beyond contingencies is a risk.

Risk #4. Balance Sheet & Cash Use

While the balance sheet is currently strong, the risk is that working capital swings could consume cash. If TPC has to invest in projects (paying subcontractors and suppliers) faster than it gets paid by clients, cash flow could go negative in a given period.

The company historically had to borrow to cover such swings. In fact, the new $400m bond at ~12% interest is a pricey debt; if cash flows falter, that interest is a heavy burden.

Bears might also point out that carrying large amounts of cash doesn’t guarantee shareholder returns. Management might use it in ways that don’t directly benefit shareholders (like acquisitions or just sitting idle while paying high interest on debt, effectively a negative carry). The variant view (my view) is that this is manageable, but it’s something to monitor.

Now, why I still have a positive thesis (variant view):

The typical bear case, anchored in past issues (claims, losses), is absolutely valid historically. But my variant view is that the situation has materially changed:

  • Record Backlog of Better Quality: This backlog isn’t just big, it’s different. Management notes that it has higher margins and better terms. We already saw evidence: civil margins up to 15%, minimal competition allowing selective bidding. So while execution risk remains, the cushion for error is larger now. They are no longer scraping by on 1–2% margins where any hiccup causes a loss; they’re aiming for +10% in Civil, for example, so even if something goes wrong and erodes a few points, the project can still be profitable. Essentially, I believe the risk-adjusted profitability of backlog is higher than bears assume.

  • Management’s Risk Management: The new management approach of embedding contingency and raising guidance only cautiously (and even then, factoring in unknowns) suggests they are not “betting the farm” on perfect outcomes. They clearly learned from the past. Note how in Q&A, Smalley said they advanced a settlement and released some contingency reserves from a project because it was successful. That indicates they budgeted conservatively and only recognized extra profit when truly earned. This is a big change from the old days of recognizing claims early. So I expect fewer nasty surprises from legacy project accounting. Also, they’ve largely dealt with older problem jobs (only “two jobs of any consequence in final stages” now, which any revenue drop from those is offset by ramping up new ones ). So the drag of the past is largely gone.

  • Legal outcomes may surprise on the upside, too: While we worry about losing claims, there’s also the chance of winning claims or settlements positively. Tutor Perini has some large claims in process (for example, it was pursuing over $100m on an electrical job at a NYC airport, etc.). If they win any, that could be a windfall (and likely mostly cash, since they already wrote down some of it). The Q2 cash flow included “to a much lesser extent” some dispute collections, implying maybe ~$20–30m of the $262m was from legal wins. If more come in Q3 or Q4, that’s bonus cash, not in forecasts. Granted, I’m not banking on legal wins, but it’s asymmetric: the market seems to price in only the bad outcomes (given the low valuation), while ignoring possible favourable resolutions.

  • Macro risk mitigated by funded projects: Many of Tutor Perini’s big projects are already funded or appropriated. For instance, FTA-funded transit projects have the money earmarked. Even if a recession hits, governments typically continue ongoing projects (they may halt future ones, but the backlog covers several years already). Also, infrastructure tends to get stimulus in downturns, not cuts. The variant view is that TPC’s work is relatively defensive within construction. It’s not speculative real estate development; it’s public infrastructure, largely, which tends to be more resilient. In fact, if private construction cools, Tutor Perini’s public focus looks smart. Their 2024 revenue was ~72% government; backlog is 77% state/local + 8% federal (so 85% government). That’s a stable customer base.

  • Balance sheet as a buffer: The net cash position and ongoing cash generation mean TPC can weather issues better now. In the past, when something went wrong, they had to borrow more or refinance in unfavourable times. Now they have liquidity. That reduces the risk of a crisis (no near debt maturities either). If a project needs cash, they have it. If an opportunity arises, they can fund it. So I’m less worried about insolvency or desperation moves, which were slight concerns a couple of years back.

In the bear case scenario, maybe Tutor Perini struggles to consistently turn backlog into profit, making only, say, $1 EPS each year. In that case, the stock might languish or drop if a loss reappears.

But I think the chance of returning to multi-year losses is low now, barring a black swan event like a catastrophic project failure. The tide has turned: backlog composition changed, management practices changed, and industry dynamics changed in their favour.

My variant view is essentially that the market is extrapolating past problems into the future, while I see a fundamentally improved set-up. This is why the stock can re-rate and why I’m bullish even after a big YTD run-up.

So yes, Tutor Perini is not a risk-free stock; it requires trust in a turnaround. But I believe the downside risks are outweighed by the upside potential given the transformation underway.

Catalysts

A few catalysts could unlock the value in Tutor Perini or drive the stock higher over the next 12–18 months:

Catalyst #1. Earnings Surprises to the Upside

The most immediate catalyst is continued strong quarterly results. Q3 and Q4 2025 earnings, if they show high revenue growth, good margins, and solid cash flow, will further prove the turnaround.

Management has set a relatively conservative bar (GAAP EPS $1.70–$2.00 for 2025). If they beat that, the market will take notice.

For instance, in Q2 they beat expectations ($0.38 GAAP EPS vs $0.02 a year prior) and the stock jumped ~34% from $47 to $63.

Another beat in Q3 (scheduled for early Nov 2025) could have a similar effect.

Additionally, hitting or exceeding the new adjusted EPS range ($3.65–$3.95) will build confidence that this level of profitability is real.

Catalyst #2. New Contract Wins (especially signature projects)

While the backlog is huge, each new marquee award reminds investors of growth ahead. For example, if Tutor Perini wins a piece of a major upcoming project, say a big section of the Gateway Tunnel in NY/NJ, or another large federal project, it could be a catalyst.

They mentioned significant opportunities in L.A., Indo-Pacific region, Midwest, etc. News of a multi-hundred-million or billion-dollar contract in one of those areas would likely boost the stock, as it implies further backlog growth and revenue visibility. The company often issues press releases for contract wins. Even smaller awards in aggregate show momentum.

Catalyst #3. Backlog Monetization Events

One interesting catalyst is if some portion of the backlog moves from pre-construction to full go-ahead. They mentioned several Building projects in pre-construction that will convert to backlog in 2025.

When those convert, the backlog could bump up again or at least become more concrete. The market might view that as de-risking. Similarly, if any public-private partnership projects reach financial close (meaning all funding secured), that locks in backlog.

For example, if Tutor Perini is part of a shortlisted PPP that reaches closing, they can add to the backlog and start work. This tends to come in bursts and can be announced.

Catalyst #4. Resolution of Legacy Claims

A positive legal outcome could be a catalyst. If one quarter they announce a settlement of a big dispute with a developer or agency that results in a cash payment, that would not only bring in cash but also remove an overhang. It would signal that the worst of the legal cloud is over.

The Q2 call Q&A had an analyst asking about “major project closeouts”. The response was that only 2 old jobs are left in the final stages, and any revenue decline from them is offset by new jobs.

If by Q4 they can say “those two are done and we settled any claims on them,” it’s psychologically important. The market currently assigns a bit of a “claims discount” to TPC; lifting that could help multiples.

Catalyst #5. Shareholder-Friendly Moves

While I don’t expect a dividend immediately, any hint of capital return could be a catalyst. For instance, if in 2026 the company initiates a modest dividend or buyback due to strong cash and earnings, that might attract a new class of investors (income funds, etc.).

Even before that, improving the credit rating or refinancing the 11.875% debt at a lower rate (if market conditions allow late 2025 or 2026) would be a catalyst by reducing interest costs further. Essentially, any move that shows the company’s risk profile is lower (like a credit upgrade or debt paydown) could bump the stock.

Catalyst #6. Industry Recognition & Coverage

Tutor Perini has been under-followed (only a few analysts cover it, from small firms).

If one of the bigger banks or research shops initiates coverage or upgrades the stock, that could draw attention. Also, TPC might appear on more investors’ screens as a top performer (it’s been one of the best small-cap stocks in 2025 so far).

Sometimes inclusion in “top stock picks” lists or positive media (e.g., an Investor’s Business Daily feature on infrastructure stocks) can act as a minor catalyst. Given that it’s a turnaround story, as each quarter confirms the trend, you may see more bullish commentary emerge.

Verdict: From Underdog to Top Pick

This deep dive has shown a company that endured a rough past but is now hitting its stride. With a transformed backlog, rising margins, and a management team steering toward prudent growth, Tutor Perini is poised to deliver substantial earnings in the coming years.

At around $60, the stock offers significant upside to my $92 fair value estimate. There are risks in any construction business, but I believe these are outweighed by the unique opportunity to own one of the few contractors capable of building America’s next-generation infrastructure… at a very reasonable price.
